In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of a complex glandular architecture and/or the presence of a solid growth pattern in a low-grade endometroid carcinoma should raise suspicion of a serous carcinoma, especially if it is accompanied by a high mitotic count and/or a high proliferation index.

endometrioid carcinomas of endometrium are characterized by the presence of a glandular pattern, a well-developed endometrial glandular architecture, a low mitotic count (usually <10 mitoses/10 high-power fields), a low Ki-67 proliferation index, a low-grade nuclear grade (usually grade 1), a low nuclear atypia, the presence of psammoma bodies, and an absence of a desmoplastic stromal reaction.
low-grade endometrial endometrioid carcinomas and low-grade serous carcinomas are different entities with different prognoses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

low-grade endometroid carcinoma and serous endometrial carcinoma are 2 distinct entities that can be reliably separated on the basis of their clinical, morphologic and immunohistochemcial characteristics.
low-grade endometrial carcinomas are characterized by a low mitotic count, a low proliferation rate, and a low rate of apoptosis and necrosis, and are typically associated with a good prognosis.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a low-grade endometrial cancer is unlikely to be a serous carcinoma.
